title: The white wines on the exam
lead: The eight white grapes the Court can pour at Certified level, with their exam regions and how each one shows up on the grid.

intro.title: READ THE FINE PRINT
intro.text: The Court's list fixes more than the grape. For several whites it also sets the sweetness or the oak, which is a clue in itself.

sections.name: Albariño

lines.label: On the exam
lines.text: Unoaked Albariño from Rías Baixas, in Spain's cool, humid, Atlantic northwest.

lines.label: On the grid
lines.text: Citrus and stone fruit, high acidity, a salty finish, and often a light bitter note from its thick skins.

know: The exam's Albariño is Rías Baixas, with no oak.
Fruit: grapefruit, lime, nectarine; honeysuckle in the background.
Structure: high acidity, light body, 11.5-13.5% alcohol.
Thick skins can leave a pith or almond bitterness (phenolic bitterness).
Compare it with Pinot Grigio, as the Court suggests.

sections.name: Chardonnay

lines.label: On the exam
lines.text: Burgundy at Village or Premier Cru level: Chablis (no new oak), Côte de Beaune and Mâconnais (new oak). California: Napa, Sonoma, Central Coast, new oak.

lines.label: On the grid
lines.text: Apple or citrus runs through every style. Oak, malolactic and lees decide the rest.

know: Burgundy entries are Village or Premier Cru only.
Chablis: no new oak; tart green apple, lemon, chalky mineral, high acid.
Côte de Beaune and Mâconnais: new oak; riper fruit, butter, toast.
California: new oak; riper stone and tropical fruit, fuller body.
Gold color often means oak: oxygen in the barrel deepens it.

lines.label: On the grid
lines.text: Smells sweet and floral, tastes dry; peach and citrus with lively acidity and no oak.

know: The exam's Torrontés is from Salta or Mendoza, Argentina.
Smells sweet (rose, geranium, peach) but is usually dry.
Court: highly aromatic, medium-plus to high acidity, usually no oak.
A Muscat of Alexandria offspring, which explains the perfume.

mixups.why: Both cool and mineral: Chablis is Chardonnay (apple, lemon, no pyrazines); Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc (grass, gooseberry, flint).
Both off-dry with high acid: Vouvray shows quince and a fuller body; Riesling shows lime, petrol and low alcohol.
Both perfumed: Gewurztraminer is lychee, low acid and off-dry; Torrontés is peach and geranium, dry, with lively acid.
Pouilly-Fumé is Loire Sauvignon Blanc; Pouilly-Fuissé is a Mâconnais Chardonnay.

sources: Court of Master Sommeliers Americas: Certified-Level examinable wines list (9.2025), Certified exam guide, Certified tasting grid and the Curriculum Guide; official bodies (BIVB, Chablis, Vins de Loire, Centre-Loire, Vins d'Alsace, Wines of Germany, New Zealand Winegrowers); grape profiles from Wine Folly. Checked Nov 2, 2026.

facts.fact: Certified white examinable wines: Albarino (Spain, Rias Baixas, no oak); Chardonnay (France, Burgundy: Chablis no new oak, Cote de Beaune new oak, Maconnais new oak, Village or Premier Cru only; United States, California: Napa Valley, Sonoma County, Central Coast, new oak); Chenin Blanc (Loire, Vouvray, demi-sec/off-dry only); Gewurztraminer (France, Alsace, off-dry only); Pinot Grigio (Italy, Friuli / Trentino-Alto Adige); Riesling (Germany, Mosel / Rheingau, Kabinett or Spatlese, off-dry only); Sauvignon Blanc (Loire: Sancerre / Pouilly-Fume; New Zealand: Marlborough); Torrontes (Argentina, Salta / Mendoza).
Expected skill set of a Certified Sommelier: 'Deductive Tasting Method ability for core classic red and white varieties'.
Prep: taste examples of all Certified examinable grapes and regions and practice writing out grids for each.

White comparisons the Court suggests: Vouvray and German Riesling; Chablis and Sancerre; California Chardonnay, Chablis and oaked Cote d'Or Chardonnay; Pinot Grigio and Chablis; Gewurztraminer and Torrontes; New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc and Sancerre; Albarino and Pinot Grigio.

White grid: color Straw, Yellow, Gold; fruit lines Apple/Pear, Citrus, Stone Fruit, Tropical; non-fruit lines include Flowers, Green Bell Pepper/Grass, Grape Variety Spice, Noble Rot, Lees, Malolactic, Petrol, Mineral, New Oak; structure: Phenolic Bitterness, Sweetness (Dry, Off-Dry), Acidity, Alcohol; white age ranges 1-2, 3-4, 5+ years.
Exam guide example: a Gewurztraminer may have some apple/pear, but tropical is very apparent and key, so No for apple/pear and Yes for tropical with descriptors such as pineapple, mango, banana.
If you called the wine off-dry and chose Sauvignon Blanc, look back for where things went off-track.
Wayne Belding, MS (quoted): Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc and Argentine Torrontes rose from non-existent to classic in a few decades.
Albarino: primary flavors lemon zest, grapefruit, honeydew, nectarine, saline; dry, light body, high acidity, 11.5-13.5% ABV.

Albarino nose: nectarine, lime, grapefruit, subtle honeysuckle. Palate: weighty mid-palate, mouthwatering acidity, finishing with salinity and sometimes a subtle bitter note (green almond or citrus pith).
Albarino grapes are tiny with thick skins, giving a raw-almond or citrus-pith bitterness from the skin's phenols. Albarino performs well in cool and intermediate climates such as Galicia.
Rias Baixas (Court, Introductory): northwest Iberian Peninsula; maritime, humid, cooler than the rest of Spain; Atlantic Ocean.
Rias Baixas winemaking (Court): modern technology, stainless steel, lees aging common; dry, crisp, aromatic whites; Albarino-labelled wines must be 100% Albarino.
Court (Certified column): Albarino is a classic match for simply prepared shellfish; high canopy trellising because of humidity; granite soil.
Chardonnay: unoaked or Chablis shows green apple, pear, citrus, with chalky or mineral aromas; unoaked styles are lean and crisp with high acidity.

Oaked, Burgundian-style Chardonnay: peach, mango, lemon with vanilla and butter; oak, malolactic fermentation and lees contact add nutty character and toasted bread; fuller body, creamy, moderate acidity, baking spices over stone fruit. Both styles share apple or citrus.
Chablis: lean, steely, flinty-mineral edge, cooler climate and minimal oak; tart green apple, lemon and oyster shell; a yogurt aroma from malolactic fermentation.

Cote d'Or Chardonnay: most wines undergo oak aging, malolactic fermentation and lees stirring; warmer, fuller wines than Chablis. Napa Chardonnay: richer stone fruit and tropical tones, full-bodied, generous oak aging, buttery and toasty.
Oaked Chardonnay wines are often gold in color due to oxygen during oak aging. With age, Chardonnay tends to develop hazelnut aromas.
Chablis soils: Kimmeridgian limestone and marl with small oyster fossils.
Chablis is mainly semi-continental and prone to spring frost; the Maconnais is hotter and drier, with Mediterranean influence.
Cote de Beaune: from Meursault south, Chardonnay dominates; Grands Crus include Montrachet and Corton-Charlemagne.
Maconnais: Chardonnay is 80% of vines; village appellations include Pouilly-Fuisse and Saint-Veran.
California (Court): often extensive use of new French and sometimes American oak; malolactic fermentation often used for white wines, especially Chardonnay.
Chenin Blanc: primary flavors quince, yellow apple, pear, chamomile, honey; dry (profile), medium-light body, high acidity, 11.5-13.5% ABV.

Chenin Blanc nose: quince, apple or apple-skin aromas; later picking or noble rot brings ripe pineapple, orange peel, honey, dried chamomile. Palate: high acidity no matter the style; 'Riesling's acidity meets Chardonnay's body and texture'.

Vouvray produces off-dry (demi-sec) to sweet Chenin Blanc with quince, honey and ripe pear, a fuller body and balanced acidity. Chenin ripens unevenly, which allows dry, off-dry and (with noble rot) sweet wines.
Vouvray: grape Chenin; still white and sparkling; styles dry, sweet and sparkling; 7 communes on the right bank of the Loire.
Loire sweet whites come from botrytis (noble rot) or passerillage on late-picked Chenin; Vouvray moelleux is among them.
The Loire Valley, in northern France, is a cool-climate growing region.
Gewurztraminer: primary flavors lychee, rose, grapefruit, tangerine, ginger; off-dry (profile), medium body, low acidity, 13.5-15% ABV.

Gewurztraminer nose: distinctive lychee and rose, with ginger, orange blossom and delicate spice. Palate: medium to full body, sometimes slightly oily, higher alcohol as it ripens quickly; acidity moderate to low.

Gewurztraminer's name comes from the German 'Gewurz', meaning spice; its spice-driven character comes largely from terpenes; lychee comes from linalool. Its pink skins can give the wine a golden tinge.
Alsace is the adopted homeland of Gewurztraminer, with over a quarter of plantings; Alsace AOC Gewurztraminer ranges from dry to off-dry.
Sheltered by the Vosges, Alsace has one of France's lowest rainfalls and a sunny, warm, dry semi-continental climate.

Pinot Gris/Grigio: primary flavors white peach, lemon zest, cantaloupe, green almond, crushed gravel; dry, medium-light body, medium-high acidity, 11.5-13.5% ABV. It is a color mutation of Pinot Noir with pinkish-gray skins.

Italian Pinot Grigio is usually totally dry with brilliant acidity and a bitter almond note, normally the lightest and freshest style; the best examples come from the Alpine foothills rather than the flat Venetian plain.
Court: Trentino-Alto Adige and Friuli are cool continental with the Alps; both make single-variety wines with the grape on the label.
Riesling: primary flavors lime, green apple, beeswax, jasmine, petroleum; off-dry, light body, high acidity, under 10% ABV.
Riesling often shows a petrol or petroleum-wax aroma from the natural compound TDN.

Mosel Riesling: pale straw, deepening to yellow with age; young wines show lime and honeydew, sometimes mineral notes; with age, honey, apricot, Meyer lemon and petrol. Intensely high acidity, usually balanced with some sweetness. The Mosel is a cool-climate region with slate soils.
Kabinett: fine, light wines from ripe grapes with low alcohol. Spatlese: harvested a little later, more intense, not necessarily sweet.
Mosel (Court): porous, heat-retaining slate; south-facing vineyards. Rheingau (Court): a long south-facing slope facing the Rhine, mountains protect it from the cold north.
Rheingau has the highest percentage of Riesling of any German region; Johannisberg is the birthplace of Spatlese (1775).

Sauvignon Blanc: primary flavors gooseberry, honeydew, grapefruit, white peach, passion fruit; dry, medium-light body, high acidity, 11.5-13.5% ABV. Green aromatics come from methoxypyrazines; nose ranges from cut grass, peas and asparagus to passion fruit and grapefruit.

Loire Sauvignon Blanc: lime, gooseberry, grapefruit, flint, smoke; mineral-driven, often slightly smoky, citrus and grassy. Sancerre: vibrant, mineral and citrus. Pouilly-Fume: similar weight, often slightly softer, with gunflint.

Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc: passion fruit, lime, gooseberry, pea shoot; vibrant fruit and razor-sharp acidity; a gram or two of residual sugar is normal because acids are so high; bell pepper, tomato stalk and cut grass.
New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc shows red capsicum, gooseberry and passionfruit; Marlborough's first Sauvignon Blanc vines were planted in 1975.

Sauvignon Blanc on the palate: light-bodied with racy acidity and moderate alcohol. The Loire's cool climate produces a fruity, tart wine. A vein of Kimmeridgian soil runs through the Loire as well as Champagne and Chablis; Sancerre's terres blanches mix clay, Kimmeridgian limestone and oyster shells.
Marlborough has a cool yet high-sunshine climate with low rainfall; it is New Zealand's largest region.
Alsace Pinot Gris: a rich, full-bodied style with ripe orchard and tropical fruit and refreshing acidity.
Sancerre: white from Sauvignon Blanc on the left bank of the Loire; soils terres blanches, caillottes and siliceous clay.
Pouilly-Fume is Sauvignon Blanc (Centre-Loire), not Pouilly-Fuisse (Burgundy Chardonnay).

Torrontes: primary flavors Meyer lemon, peach, rose petal, geranium, citrus zest; dry, medium-light body; smells sweet but usually made dry. Torrontes Riojano is an offspring of Muscat of Alexandria and the most widely planted and highest-quality type.
Some of the most distinctive Torrontes comes from high-elevation vineyards in Salta, particularly the Calchaqui Valleys around Cafayate.
Court: Torrontes is highly aromatic with soapy, floral and fruity flavors and medium-plus to high acidity; commonly no oak.
Court: Salta (subregion Cafayate) is known for Torrontes; Salta is 1,500-2,000 m, the highest in Argentina; Mendoza is 600-1,200 m.

unverified: Typical grape profiles (fruit, acidity, alcohol) come from Wine Folly, not the Court, and vary by producer.
Wine Folly gives Torrontés medium acidity; the Court's Curriculum Guide says medium-plus to high. The chapter uses the Court's call.
The climate calls in the grid tiles (e.g. Albariño cool to moderate) are drawn from region descriptions, not from a Court answer key.
The Court's Grape Variety Profiles PDF (GuildSomm) could not be read as text, so its white-grape details were not used here.
No Wine Folly, Court or official video focused on Chenin Blanc was found; the Torrontés section uses Wine Folly's general Argentina video.

read.bigIdea: Albariño: Atlantic citrus with a salty, bitter edge.
read.where: The Court's Albariño comes from **Rías Baixas**, in Spain's northwest. It's maritime and humid, cooler than the rest of Spain, and the exam wine has **no oak**. Stainless steel and lees aging are common there.

stops.name: Nose
stops.text: **Citrus** (grapefruit, lime) and **stone fruit** (nectarine), with a hint of honeysuckle.

stops.name: Palate
stops.text: Dry, light-bodied, with mouthwatering **high acidity** and a salty finish. Its thick skins can leave a **citrus-pith or almond bitterness**: think **phenolic bitterness**.

stops.name: Conclusion
stops.text: **Spain**. Wine Folly says Albariño does well in **cool and intermediate** climates like Galicia, so cool or moderate.

read.mixup: **Albariño** shows grapefruit, nectarine and salinity. **Pinot Grigio** shows white peach, lemon zest and green almond.
read.sayIt: A crisp coastal white from Spain. Perfect with shellfish.

read.bigIdea: One grape, three styles: tell them apart by oak and fruit.
read.where: The Court lists **Burgundy** at **Village or Premier Cru** level (**Chablis** with no new oak, **Côte de Beaune** and **Mâconnais** with new oak) and **California** (Napa, Sonoma, Central Coast) with **new oak**. Every style shares apple or citrus; the winemaking tells you which one you have.

stops.name: Chablis
stops.text: Tart **green apple**, **lemon**, oyster shell and a chalky, mineral edge from **Kimmeridgian** soils. Lean, with **high acidity**. A yogurt note from malolactic can show.

stops.name: Côte de Beaune · Mâconnais
stops.text: Most Côte d'Or Chardonnay sees **oak**, **malolactic** and **lees stirring**: riper fruit, **vanilla**, **butter**, **toast** and nutty notes. The Mâconnais is hotter and drier than Chablis.

stops.name: California
stops.text: Napa leans to **stone and tropical fruit**, a **full body** and generous **new oak**, with buttery, toasty notes from malolactic.

read.mixup: **Lees** smell like bread and dough. **Malolactic** smells like butter, cream and yogurt.
read.sayIt: Chablis is the crisp, unoaked Chardonnay. Meursault-style and California are rounder and toastier.

read.bigIdea: Chenin Blanc: quince and honey over bright acidity.
read.where: The exam's Chenin is **Vouvray**, from Touraine in the **Loire**, and only the **demi-sec (off-dry)** style. Chenin ripens unevenly, which is how one grape can make dry, off-dry and sweet wines.

stops.name: Nose
stops.text: **Quince**, **yellow apple** and **pear**, with **chamomile** and **honey**. Riper or botrytised grapes add pineapple, orange peel and more honey.

stops.name: Palate
stops.text: **Off-dry**, with **high acidity** in every style. Wine Folly puts it as Riesling's acidity with Chardonnay's body.

stops.name: Conclusion
stops.text: **France**, from the **cool** Loire Valley. If honey and ginger are key, the **noble rot** line may be a Yes.

read.mixup: **Vouvray** is Chenin Blanc with quince and a fuller body. **German Riesling** is lighter, with lime and petrol.

read.bigIdea: Pinot Grigio: light, dry, peachy, with a bitter twist.
read.where: The exam's Pinot Grigio comes from **Friuli** or **Trentino-Alto Adige**, both **cool continental**, shaped by the Alps. Both make single-variety wines with the grape on the label. Pinot Grigio is a **color mutation of Pinot Noir**.

stops.name: Nose
stops.text: **White peach**, **lemon zest** and **melon**, with a stony, crushed-gravel note.

stops.name: Palate
stops.text: Usually fully **dry**, light, with **bright acidity** and a **bitter almond** finish.

stops.name: Conclusion
stops.text: **Italy**, cool climate. Wine Folly says the best come from the **Alpine foothills**, not the flat Venetian plain.

read.mixup: **Pinot Grigio** is the Italian name and style: light and dry. **Pinot Gris** in Alsace is richer and fuller.

read.bigIdea: Riesling: lime, petrol and acidity you can't miss.
read.where: The exam's Riesling is German, from the **Mosel** or **Rheingau**, at **Kabinett** or **Spätlese** level, **off-dry** only. The Mosel's steep, south-facing **slate** slopes and the Rheingau's long south-facing slope above the Rhine help grapes ripen in a cool climate.

stops.name: Look
stops.text: Pale **straw** when young, deepening to yellow with age.

stops.name: Nose
stops.text: **Lime**, **green apple**, **jasmine**; with age, honey, apricot and **petrol** (the compound **TDN**).

stops.name: Palate
stops.text: **Off-dry**, **high acidity**, light body and **low alcohol**. Kabinett is the lightest; Spätlese is picked later and is more intense.

read.mixup: **Spätlese** means late harvest, not necessarily sweet. **Kabinett** is lighter and lower in alcohol.
read.sayIt: Light and bright, with a touch of sweetness. Great with spicy food.

read.bigIdea: Sauvignon Blanc: green, zesty, and two very different homes.
read.where: The Court lists two homes: the **Loire** (**Sancerre**, **Pouilly-Fumé**) and **New Zealand** (**Marlborough**). Both are cool, and both show the grape's **pyrazine** green notes and **high acidity**. The Court pairs them as a must-compare.

stops.name: Sancerre · Pouilly-Fumé
stops.text: **Lime**, **grapefruit**, **gooseberry**, with **flint**, **smoke** and mineral notes. Pouilly-Fumé is often a bit softer, with gunflint.

stops.name: Marlborough
stops.text: Pungent **passion fruit**, **gooseberry**, **bell pepper** and cut grass, with **razor-sharp acidity**. A gram or two of sugar is normal because the acidity is so high.

stops.name: The cross-check
stops.text: If your notes say **off-dry** and you're about to write Sauvignon Blanc, the Court says to look back for where things went off-track.

read.mixup: **Pouilly-Fumé** is Loire Sauvignon Blanc. **Pouilly-Fuissé** is Burgundy Chardonnay.

read.bigIdea: Torrontés: a perfumed nose and a dry, lively palate.
read.where: The exam's Torrontés comes from **Salta** or **Mendoza**, Argentina. Salta's vineyards sit at **1,500-2,000 m**, the highest in the country, and Cafayate is known for it. Torrontés Riojano is an offspring of **Muscat of Alexandria**.

stops.name: Nose
stops.text: **Rose petal**, **geranium**, **peach**, Meyer lemon and citrus zest. The Court calls it highly aromatic, even soapy.

stops.name: Palate
stops.text: Usually **dry**, despite the sweet smell, with **medium-plus to high acidity** (the Court's call) and commonly **no oak**.

stops.name: Conclusion
stops.text: **Argentina**. It's one of the wines the Court names as becoming a classic within a few decades.

read.mixup: **Torrontés** is dry, with lively acid. **Gewurztraminer** on the exam is off-dry, with low acid.
